items.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Right. I guess the Joshua Redman and Christian McBride and that, those younger players, they do standards...

ctx.x: I wish I knew. If it’s a matter of making money I can understand, because I don’t know any wealthy jazz musicians. But I don’t know lots of white musicians who’ve played blues or soul who have overseas tours and make lots of recordings. And you know I think it’s a matter of going where the money is, and I can’t blame anyone for that. I wish there were more black players, but the ones who play it tend to like, really, more modern styles — mainstream and beyond — rather than the earlier styles.

Right. I guess the Joshua Redman and Christian McBride and that, those younger players, they do standards, but then they’re more into I guess their own music, kind of breaking — I don’t know if they’re breaking ground or not.

They probably are. And I think there’s a number of musicians who play traditional jazz in concerts and tours and make recordings, but given their choice of what to play, that would not be what they want to play. They can make a certain good living doing that, but that’s not their music. And I’ve witnessed that time and again. I know a trombone player in New Orleans, Freddie Lonzo, who is one of the few black players I’ve heard who really digs into the style and likes the style and is not on the bandstand like…
